subject: film
title: Feminist film theory and women's cinema, 1972 to 1992
dek: In 1972 two festivals, one in New York and one in Edinburgh, showed audiences something most of them had never seen in one place: decades of films directed by women. Over the next twenty years critics asked why women on screen so often existed only to be looked at, theorists like Laura Mulvey gave that problem a name, the male gaze, and directors such as Chantal Akerman, Agnès Varda and Sally Potter made films that refused to look at women the old way. This lesson covers the ideas, the films and the arguments, and ends in Taipei, where a women's film festival began in 1993 and is still run today by one of the organisations on Huiru's partner list.
era: c. 1972 to 1992, with roots in the 1960s women's movement
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in Wikipedia articles on the films, critics and festivals, the BFI's report on the 2022 Sight and Sound poll, the 1972 New York Times notice of the New York festival, Edinburgh festival histories, and the Taiwan Women's Film Association's own history page. Quotations from Mulvey come from the published text of her 1975 essay. Where a detail could not be checked, it was left out. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

fun_fact.title: A joke that became a measuring stick
fun_fact.text: The Bechdel test began in 1985 as a single strip in Alison Bechdel's comic Dykes to Watch Out For, printed in alternative and feminist newspapers. In the strip, called 'The Rule', one woman explains that she only goes to a film if it has at least two women in it, who talk to each other, about something other than a man. Bechdel credited the idea to her friend Liz Wallace, and it also echoes Virginia Woolf's complaint in A Room of One's Own (1929) that women in fiction are almost always shown only in relation to men. Bechdel later called it a little lesbian joke in an alternative feminist newspaper. By the 2000s critics, journalists and researchers were using it to count films, which is why it is now often called the Bechdel–Wallace test.

sections.title: Before 1972: women behind the camera, mostly forgotten

blocks.text: Women were present at the start of cinema. In France, Alice Guy, who worked for the Gaumont company, is often credited with one of the earliest fiction films, around 1896, and went on to run her own studio in the United States. In the Hollywood of the 1910s, Lois Weber was one of the most successful directors in the business and made films about birth control and abortion such as Where Are My Children? (1916). When the studios became big industrial businesses in the 1920s and 1930s, these jobs largely closed to women. For much of the 1930s Dorothy Arzner was the only woman directing features inside the studio system, with films like Dance, Girl, Dance (1940). In the 1950s the actress Ida Lupino directed low-budget dramas and The Hitch-Hiker (1953), usually described as the first mainstream American film noir directed by a woman.

Outside Hollywood, women made some of the most adventurous films of the century. Maya Deren's short Meshes of the Afternoon (1943), made with Alexander Hammid, became a founding work of the American avant-garde. Agnès Varda made her first feature in 1955, before the French New Wave had a name, and Cléo from 5 to 7 (1962) follows a young singer through ninety minutes of a Paris afternoon while she waits for a cancer test result. In Czechoslovakia, Věra Chytilová's Daisies (1966) showed two young women wrecking a banquet. In the Soviet Union, Larisa Shepitko made Wings (1966) about a former fighter pilot who cannot fit into peacetime life.

Yet in the 1960s there was no shared story of women's cinema. Histories of film were written as lists of great male directors, and the few women in them looked like exceptions. That changed when the second wave of the women's movement reached film culture. Books like Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) had already asked how mass media shaped women's lives. In 1971 the Manifesto of the 343, in which French women declared that they had had illegal abortions, was signed by film people including Agnès Varda and the actress Delphine Seyrig. Feminists began asking the same questions of cinema that they asked of law and the family: who makes it, who is shown, and whose interests does it serve.

sections.title: 1972: the year women's cinema became visible

blocks.text: Two events in 1972 gave the new movement a public face. From 5 to 21 June the First International Festival of Women's Films ran at the Fifth Avenue Cinema in New York. According to the New York Times notice that May, it showed 13 features, 4 documentary features and 13 programmes of shorts, including Dorothy Arzner's The Wild Party (1929), Ida Lupino's The Bigamist (1953), Varda's Cléo from 5 to 7 and Barbara Loden's Wanda.

Two months later, at the Edinburgh International Film Festival in Scotland, Lynda Myles, Laura Mulvey and Claire Johnston programmed a season of more than 30 films made by women between 1923 and 1972. It ran from Germaine Dulac's The Smiling Madame Beudet (1923) and Leontine Sagan's Girls in Uniform (1931) through Arzner, Lupino, Deren and Chytilová. It was the first event of its kind in Europe. A year later Myles became the festival's director, which the festival describes as the first time a woman ran an international film festival anywhere.

The same year saw the first issue of the journal Women and Film in California and the founding of Women Make Movies, a New York group that taught women filmmaking and later became one of the main distributors of films by women. In West Germany the director Helke Sander founded Frauen und Film (Women and Film) in 1974, and in the United States the journal Camera Obscura began in 1976. Within a few years there was a network of festivals, journals and distributors where none had existed before.

Barbara Loden's Wanda (1970), which both festivals showed, explains why this mattered. Loden, an actress married to the director Elia Kazan, wrote, directed and starred in it for about $115,000. Wanda is a passive, broke woman from a Pennsylvania coal town who leaves her husband and children and drifts into a partnership with a small-time bank robber. The film won the Pasinetti award for best foreign film at Venice in 1970 but had little distribution in the United States. Loden died of cancer in 1980, and Wanda was her only feature. Today it is regarded as a classic, an example of how a film can disappear when there are no institutions to keep it in view.

sections.title: From images of women to the male gaze

blocks.text: The first wave of feminist film criticism, in the early 1970s, mostly looked at images of women. Marjorie Rosen's Popcorn Venus (1973) and Molly Haskell's From Reverence to Rape (1974) traced how Hollywood showed women decade by decade. Haskell, a critic in New York, argued that the strong career women played by actresses such as Bette Davis and Katharine Hepburn in the 1930s and 1940s had given way to weaker and more sexualised roles, and that American films of the early 1970s were among the worst for women. This approach asked whether a character was a positive or negative image, a stereotype or a real person.

British critics close to the journal Screen thought this did not go far enough. In 'Women's Cinema as Counter-Cinema' (1973), Claire Johnston argued that the problem was not just bad characters but the language of mainstream cinema itself. In Hollywood films, she wrote, woman works as a sign, a fixed idea that stands for what men want or fear, rather than as a person. She also suggested that some women directors inside the studio system, especially Arzner, had found ways to make that language visible from the inside. Johnston and Pam Cook developed this argument in a 1975 BFI book on Arzner.

Laura Mulvey went further. Her essay 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema', published in Screen in the autumn of 1975, used ideas from Freud and Lacan to ask why classical Hollywood films are pleasurable to watch, and for whom. Its main claims can be put simply:

items: Looking is itself a pleasure. Mulvey used Freud's term scopophilia, the pleasure of looking at another person as an object, and argued that cinema is built to provide it, since the audience sits in the dark and watches people who cannot look back.

That pleasure is split by gender. In her best-known sentence, 'In a world ordered by sexual imbalance, pleasure in looking has been split between active/male and passive/female.' The man looks and acts; the woman is displayed.
Women on screen carry what she called to-be-looked-at-ness. They are lit, framed and costumed as spectacle, and the story often stops so the camera can dwell on them, as in a showgirl's number.

Cinema combines three looks: the camera's, the characters' and the audience's. Classical films hide the first and last, so the audience identifies with the male hero's look at the woman. This structure is what later writers called the male gaze.
Her examples were the films of Josef von Sternberg with Marlene Dietrich and Alfred Hitchcock's Rear Window, Vertigo and Marnie, in which the hero watches, follows and investigates a woman.

blocks.text: Mulvey did not want to improve Hollywood. She wanted to break its pleasure on purpose. The essay says so plainly: 'It is said that analysing pleasure, or beauty, destroys it. That is the intention of this article.' She called for a counter-cinema that would free the camera's look and make the audience aware of how it was watching. With her partner Peter Wollen she made films on those lines, most famously Riddles of the Sphinx (1977), a slow, partly abstract film about a mother in London trying to arrange childcare.

sections.title: The filmmakers: many ways to look differently

blocks.text: Feminist filmmakers did not follow one style. Some made essay films and experimental work in the spirit of Mulvey and Wollen. Yvonne Rainer, a dancer from New York, made Film About a Woman Who... (1974), which breaks up a love story with on-screen text and narration. Sally Potter's short Thriller (1979) retells the opera La Bohème from the point of view of Mimì, the seamstress who dies at the end, and asks why she had to die. Potter's feature The Gold Diggers (1983), starring Julie Christie, was made by an all-woman crew. Barbara Hammer made some of the first openly lesbian experimental films, including Dyketactics (1974).

Others worked closer to art-house storytelling. In West Germany, Helke Sander's The All-Round Reduced Personality (1978), often called Redupers, follows a single mother working as a photographer in West Berlin, and Margarethe von Trotta's Marianne and Juliane (1981), about two sisters, one a journalist and one a militant, won the Golden Lion at Venice. In France, Varda's One Sings, the Other Doesn't (1977) follows two friends through the abortion rights campaigns of the 1970s, and her Vagabond (1985), about a young woman found frozen in a ditch, won the Golden Lion. In the Netherlands, Marleen Gorris's A Question of Silence (1982) shows three women who kill a shopkeeper and the psychiatrist who tries to understand them. In the Soviet Union, Larisa Shepitko's war film The Ascent won the Golden Bear in Berlin in 1977.

Some made political genre films. Lizzie Borden's Born in Flames (1983) imagines an American socialist government ten years after a peaceful revolution, under which women still face harassment and unemployment. Groups of Black, Latina, lesbian and white women argue over tactics and form militias and pirate radio stations. It was shot cheaply in New York, and its arguments about which women a movement speaks for anticipated the debates of the next decade.

Documentary was just as important. Delphine Seyrig, one of the best-known actresses in Europe after Last Year at Marienbad (1961), learned video with Carole Roussopoulos and Ioana Wieder. In 1982 the three founded the Centre audiovisuel Simone de Beauvoir in Paris to collect and preserve women's films and videos, an early example of a feminist media archive, which is close to Huiru's own idea of archiving everything.

sections.title: Jeanne Dielman: three days of potatoes, beds and dread

blocks.text: Chantal Akerman was born in Brussels in 1950 to a Jewish family; her mother had survived Auschwitz. She was 25 when she shot Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles in 1975. The film is about 200 minutes long. Delphine Seyrig plays a widow who lives with her teenage son in a small Brussels flat. Over three days we watch her routine in long, fixed shots, often from a single frontal position, with almost no music: she peels potatoes, makes the bed, washes up, breads veal cutlets, buys buttons, and in the afternoons, while the potatoes boil, has sex with a male client for money. The cinematographer was Babette Mangolte, and according to the Rotterdam festival about 80 per cent of the crew were women.

The film does not use the male gaze that Mulvey described. The camera does not move in to admire Seyrig, and it does not cut away from the dull parts. The sex scenes happen behind a closed door. What the camera does show in full, in real time, is housework, the labour that most films skip in a single cut. Akerman later said the film came from watching her mother: 'It came from what I saw as a kid, all those gestures of my mother. That's why the film is so precise.'

On the second day small things begin to go wrong. Jeanne overcooks the potatoes, drops a spoon, forgets to button her housecoat, and sits idle in a chair. Because the first day was so regular, these small slips feel shocking. On the third day she kills her client with a pair of scissors and then sits at the dining table in silence for several minutes as the film ends. Critics have read the ending in many ways, as a protest against a life without freedom, as a breakdown, or as something the film refuses to explain.

When it opened in Paris in 1976, Le Monde called it the first masterpiece of the feminine in the history of the cinema. For decades it was mainly a film for festivals, universities and cinephiles. In 2022 more than 1,600 critics, scholars and programmers voted it first in Sight and Sound's once-a-decade poll of the greatest films of all time, up from 36th place in 2012. It was the first time in the poll's 70 years that a film directed by a woman came first. Hitchcock's Vertigo, one of Mulvey's main examples of the male gaze, came second. The result showed how far the questions of the 1970s had moved from the margins into the centre of film culture, and it also started arguments about whether a slow avant-garde film should top a list most people use to find films to watch.

sections.title: Who is the woman in the audience?

blocks.text: Mulvey's essay was hugely influential and quickly criticised, including by Mulvey herself. The obvious question was where women in the audience fit. If classical films ask every viewer to identify with the male hero, how do women watch, and why do so many enjoy melodramas and romances? In 1981 Mulvey published 'Afterthoughts on Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema', inspired by the western Duel in the Sun (1946), arguing that women viewers may move back and forth between identifying with the active hero and the passive heroine.

Other writers built a theory of the female spectator. Mary Ann Doane's 'Film and the Masquerade' (1982) argued that women watching films are pushed either into over-identifying with the image or into taking up a masculine position, and that femininity itself can be a mask worn for the viewer. Teresa de Lauretis's book Alice Doesn't (1984) asked how women are formed as subjects through stories and images. E. Ann Kaplan's collection Women in Film Noir (1978) showed how the femme fatale is both punished by noir plots and remembered as their most powerful figure. Tania Modleski's The Women Who Knew Too Much (1988) re-read Hitchcock to show that his films are more troubled by women than Mulvey had allowed.

The strongest criticism came from Black feminists. In 'The Oppositional Gaze: Black Female Spectators', published in her book Black Looks (1992), bell hooks pointed out that psychoanalytic film theory talked about women as if they were all white. Black women, she wrote, had rarely seen themselves on screen at all, and had learned to watch Hollywood critically, with a gaze that looked back and resisted. A year earlier Julie Dash had released Daughters of the Dust (1991), about three generations of Gullah women on a South Carolina sea island in 1902, preparing to move north. It was the first feature directed by an African American woman to receive a general theatrical release in the United States, and it showed in practice what a film made from Black women's point of view could look like.

Popular genres got new readings too. In Men, Women, and Chain Saws (1992), Carol Clover studied slasher films and named the final girl, the young woman who survives to the end and fights back. She argued that the mostly young male audiences of these films were asked to identify with her, which complicated the simple idea that men in the audience only look at women from outside. By the early 1990s the field had moved from one big theory to many arguments about race, sexuality, genre and real audiences.

sections.title: Taiwan and Asia at the same time

blocks.text: While feminist film theory grew in Britain and the United States, Taiwan was under martial law, and the women's movement there worked carefully. In 1974 呂秀蓮 Annette Lu published 新女性主義 (New Feminism), and in 1982 李元貞 and others founded the magazine that became the Awakening Foundation (婦女新知基金會). Film was part of the change. In 1981 the actress and singer Sylvia Chang 張艾嘉 produced the television anthology 十一個女人 (Eleven Women) for TTV, adapting short stories about women's lives in Taiwan. She directed one episode herself, 〈自己的天空〉, and hired young directors including Edward Yang 楊德昌, whose episode 〈浮萍〉, about a country girl chasing fame in Taipei, was his directing debut. The series is now seen as one of the starting points of Taiwan New Cinema. In 1984 曾壯祥 Tseng Chuang-hsiang filmed 殺夫 (The Woman of Wrath), adapted from 李昂 Li Ang's 1983 novella about a woman driven to kill her abusive husband. Women directors such as 黃玉珊 Huang Yu-shan, whose 落山風 (Autumn Tempest) came out in 1988, and 王小棣 Wang Shaudi also began working in this period.

In 1993 the Awakening Foundation, with the scholars and activists 李元貞, 王蘋, 張小虹 and 丁乃非, and 黃玉珊's Black and White Studio (黑白屋電影工作室), organised the first 女性影像藝術展 (Women Make Waves) at the 霍克藝術會館 art space in Taipei, showing 16 films. It grew into a regular festival. In September 1998 its organisers registered the Taipei Women's Film Association (台北市女性影像學會), with 黃玉珊 as its first chair, and in 2004 it became the national Taiwan Women's Film Association (台灣女性影像學會). Since 2012 the festival has been called the Women Make Waves International Film Festival, Taiwan, and the association describes it as the oldest issue-based film festival in Taiwan and one of the earliest women's film festivals in Asia. Since 2001 it has also toured screenings to cinemas, schools and community spaces outside Taipei. This is the 女性影像學會 on the orgs page of Huiru's feminism class site, so the history in this lesson is also background for thinking about it as a possible cool dairy partner.

Elsewhere in Asia, the Hong Kong New Wave included Ann Hui, whose first feature The Secret (1979) and later Boat People (1982) made her one of the leading directors of the region. Across the world, the United Nations declared 1975 International Women's Year and held its first world conference on women in Mexico City, the same year that Mulvey's essay and Jeanne Dielman appeared.

sections.title: Legacy: from theory to everyday vocabulary

blocks.text: Feminist film theory changed how films are taught and talked about. The term male gaze moved from an academic journal into ordinary criticism, fashion writing and social media, often used loosely to mean any sexualised image of a woman. Its opposite, the female gaze, became a popular way to describe films by women such as Céline Sciamma's Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019), which won the screenplay prize at Cannes.

Women directors also slowly reached the top prizes. Jane Campion's The Piano shared the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1993, the first time a woman won it. Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Academy Award for best director, for The Hurt Locker, in 2010. Julia Ducournau won the Palme d'Or for Titane in 2021 and Justine Triet for Anatomy of a Fall in 2023. Counting projects like the Bechdel test and studies of who directs and speaks on screen grew from the same question the 1972 festivals asked: where are the women?

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Mulvey wanted to destroy the pleasure of the male gaze, while Akerman made a film that refuses it by showing housework in real time. Think of a film or music video you love. Who is doing the looking, and who is being looked at? Would it lose something, or gain something, if it were filmed the way Jeanne Dielman is filmed?
